**George Washington's father was Augustine Washington Sr.** (born 1694 – died April 12, 1743), an American planter and merchant from Westmoreland County, Virginia.

**The father of Augustine Washington was Lawrence Washington**. Lawrence Washington (c. 1659–1698) was a militia captain and a member of the Virginia House of Burgesses. He married Mildred Warner, and they had several children including Augustine Washington.

So to directly answer your question: **Lawrence Washington** is the father of the father of George Washington.

**Augustine Washington Sr.** (1694[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustine_Washington#cite_note-birth-3) – April 12, 1743)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustine_Washington#cite_note-Facts-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustine_Washington#cite_note-bio-2) was an American planter and merchant. Born in Westmoreland County, Virginia, he was the father of 10 children, among them the first president of the United States, George Washington; soldier and politician Lawrence Washington; politician [Augustine Washington Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustine_Washington_Jr. "Augustine Washington Jr."); and politician Charles Washington. Born into the planter class of the British colony of Virginia, Washington owned several slave plantations, from which he derived the primary source of his wealth. He also speculated in land development and owned an iron mine. Although Washington never sat in the House of Burgesses, as did his own father and son, he served in various government positions in the counties where he owned land.

## Early and family life
[edit]
Augustine Washington was born in 1694 in Westmoreland County, Virginia to Mildred Warner and her husband, Capt. Lawrence Washington, a militia captain and a member of the Virginia House of Burgesses. His paternal grandparents were Lt. Col. John Washington (c.1631–1677) and his first wife, Anne Pope. His maternal grandparents owned Warner Hall and associated plantations in Gloucester County. Augustine was four years old when his father died. His mother remarried and moved the family to England, where she died when the children were still young; although their mother's will named their stepfather George Gale as their guardian, their cousin John Washington fought to have himself named the children's guardian and brought them back to Virginia.
When Washington came of age and into his inheritance in 1715, he married Jane Butler, another orphan, who had inherited about 640 acres (2.6 km 2) from her father, Caleb Butler. The young couple settled on the Bridges Creek property and had four children, only two of whom (Lawrence and Augustine Jr.) lived to adulthood. After Jane Butler's death in November 1728[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustine_Washington#cite_note-4) or 1729,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustine_Washington#cite_note-5) Washington married Mary Ball in 1731, and the couple had five children who survived to adulthood – George, Betty, Samuel, Charles, and John Augustine – and a daughter named Mildred who died in infancy.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustine_Washington#cite_note-bio-2)

## Early and family life
When he reached legal age in 1715, Augustine Washington inherited about 1,000 acres (4.0 km 2) on Bridges Creek in Westmoreland County; his sister Mildred inherited what was called the Little Hunting Creek property;[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustine_Washington#cite_note-Kenmore-6) they both inherited enslaved people. In 1718, Washington purchased land on Pope's Creek, adjoining his property on Bridges Creek, and set about establishing himself. Between 1723 and 1735, he hired a local contractor to build a house, which was probably completed about 1726 despite the contractor's death (later called Wakefield).[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustine_Washington#cite_note-Norris_p._153-7) In the same year, Washington purchased the Little Hunting Creek property from his sister Mildred.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustine_Washington#cite_note-Mildred-8)
In 1725, Augustine Washington entered into an agreement with the Principio Company of England to start an iron works on Accokeek Creek in Stafford County, and he also owned a stake in their Maryland ironworks.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustine_Washington#cite_note-Norris_p._153-7) In 1735, the family moved to the Little Hunting Creek property, which was closer to the Accokeek Furnace.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustine_Washington#cite_note-Kenmore-6)
In 1738, Augustine Washington purchased the 150-acre Strother property across the Rappahannock River (now known as Ferry Farm) and moved the family there at the end of that same year.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustine_Washington#cite_note-Kenmore-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustine_Washington#cite_note-Mildred-8)

## Early and family life
Augustine Washington was active in the Anglican Church, the local militia, and politics.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustine_Washington#cite_note-Norris_p._153-7) He took the oath as justice of the peace for the Westmoreland county court in July 1716,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustine_Washington#cite_note-9) and served as county sheriff.
Washington died on April 12, 1743.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustine_Washington#cite_note-10) After he died, his 11-year-old son George inherited the former Strother property and its slaves.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustine_Washington#cite_note-11) Because George had not reached legal age, his widowed mother Mary Ball Washington managed this property for him until he came of age. She lived on the property until 1772 when she was 64 when George moved her to a house in Fredericksburg.
Lawrence Washington inherited the Little Hunting Creek property and renamed it "Mount Vernon" to honor Admiral Edward Vernon, with whom he had served in the Royal Navy in 1741 during the Battle of Cartagena de Indias during the [War of Jenkins' Ear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_Jenkins'_Ear "War of Jenkins' Ear").
According to Augustine Sr's will, if his son Lawrence died without children, the Little Hunting Creek property would go to Augustine Jr., and Augustine Jr, in turn, would have to give up the Popes Creek property to his brother George. If Augustine Jr. did not want the Little Hunting Creek property, George would then inherit it. Upon Lawrence's death, Augustine Jr. chose Popes Creek and its slaves over the former Little Hunting Creek property. Lawrence's only surviving child, Sarah, lived until 1754; therefore, George Washington ultimately inherited the Little Hunting Creek property, which was known as Mount Vernon by that time. At his death, Augustine Washington Sr. enslaved a total of 64 people who were assigned among the various plantations.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustine_Washington#cite_note-Slavery_at_Popes_Creek_Plantation-12)

## Early and family life
Lawrence Washington's widow, Ann, had a life interest in the Little Hunting Creek plantation. Because she remarried and was not living at Mount Vernon, she leased the property to George in 1754. Upon her death in 1761, George Washington inherited the plantation outright.

Title: 15K views · 2.9K reactions | George Washington’s father, Augustine, died on April 12, 1743. George was 11 years old. When his father died, Lawerence Washington inherited Augustine’s property on Little Hunting Creek. Lawrence was George’s half-brother from Augustine’s previous marriage to Jane Butler. George Washington greatly admired and looked up to his older brother Lawrence. 

Lawrence had just finished serving as a Captain in the War of Jenkins Ear. Lawrence  respected his commander British Admiral Edward Vernon. In fact, he renamed Little Hunting Creek plantation “Mount Vernon” after Admiral Vernon. The name remains to this day. 

Mount Vernon was a neighboring property of Belvoir. By 1741, the Fairfax family was living at Belvoir. In 1743, Lawrence married Anne Fairfax, who was the daughter of Col. William Fairfax. This marriage was important for young George Washington. It meant that George was a frequent guest both at Mount Vernon and at Belvoir.

Lawrence assumed a role as mentor and father figure to George. However, Col. Fairfax also took on that role and became a very important part of George Washington’s early career. Washington frequently sought Col. Fairfax’s counsel and guidance. Lawrence died in 1752 and Col. Fairfax helped George Washington with advice during the French and Indian War. 

Lawrence’s marriage to Anne was an important link that brought George into the orbit of one of the most powerful and well connected families in colonial Virginia. 

Follow along as we continue to show the relationship of George Washington and the Fairfax family.

[An elaborate gravestone. A tribute from a grieving husband. But no name! For 210 years, Alexandria’s mysterious “Female Stranger” has inspired a question: Who was she? Her gravestone records that she died on October 14, 1816, aged 23 years and eight months. It describes a “disconsolate husband” in whose arms she “sighed out her latest breath.” Then comes the legend: a mysterious couple at Alexandria’s City Hotel, a young woman dying in Room 8, and a husband who is said to have sworn those caring for her never to reveal her name. How much of that story is true? We don’t know. Gadsby’s Tavern Museum’s research traces a newspaper account to 1866, fifty years after her death. No surviving hotel records confirm her stay. Some have suggested she was Aaron Burr’s daughter, Theodosia Burr Alston. But Theodosia disappeared at sea in 1813, nearly four years before the death recorded here. She also would have been 33, not 23. It’s a great story but highly improbable. But the legend has grown. The gravestone remains. And the woman it commemorates has never been conclusively identified. **Augustine Washington, Sr.** (12 November 1694–12 April 1743), was an British colonial American planter and iron ore miner. He was the father of George Washington, the first president of the United States. He belonged to the Colony of Virginia's landed gentry. Like his father and his sons, Washington had owned plantations which he operated by the use of enslaved labor. He also speculated in less developed land and had even operated in an iron mine. Unlike his father and his son George, Washington was never a legislator. He held various offices in the counties where he had land.
Washington's first wife was Jane Butler, who died in November of 1729. His second wife was Mary Ball Washington, the mother of George Washington. He was the son of Lawrence Washington and his wife, Mildred Gale.

When he reached legal age in 1715, Augustine Washington inherited about 1,000 acres (4.0 km 2) on Bridges Creek in Westmoreland County; his sister Mildred inherited what was called the Little Hunting Creek property;[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustine_Washington#cite_note-Kenmore-6) they both inherited enslaved people. In 1718, Washington purchased land on Pope's Creek, adjoining his property on Bridges Creek, and set about establishing himself. Between 1723 and 1735, he hired a local contractor to build a house, which was probably completed about 1726 despite the contractor's death (later called Wakefield).[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustine_Washington#cite_note-Norris_p._153-7) In the same year, Washington purchased the Little Hunting Creek property from his sister Mildred.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustine_Washington#cite_note-Mildred-8)
In 1725, Augustine Washington entered into an agreement with the Principio Company of England to start an iron works on Accokeek Creek in Stafford County, and he also owned a stake in their Maryland ironworks.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustine_Washington#cite_note-Norris_p._153-7) In 1735, the family moved to the Little Hunting Creek property, which was closer to the Accokeek Furnace.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustine_Washington#cite_note-Kenmore-6)
In 1738, Augustine Washington purchased the 150-acre Strother property across the Rappahannock River (now known as Ferry Farm) and moved the family there at the end of that same year.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustine_Washington#cite_note-Kenmore-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustine_Washington#cite_note-Mildred-8)

## Early and family life
Augustine Washington was active in the Anglican Church, the local militia, and politics.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustine_Washington#cite_note-Norris_p._153-7) He took the oath as justice of the peace for the Westmoreland county court in July 1716,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustine_Washington#cite_note-9) and served as county sheriff.
Washington died on April 12, 1743.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustine_Washington#cite_note-10) After he died, his 11-year-old son George inherited the former Strother property and its slaves.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustine_Washington#cite_note-11) Because George had not reached legal age, his widowed mother Mary Ball Washington managed this property for him until he came of age. She lived on the property until 1772 when she was 64 when George moved her to a house in Fredericksburg.
Lawrence Washington inherited the Little Hunting Creek property and renamed it "Mount Vernon" to honor Admiral Edward Vernon, with whom he had served in the Royal Navy in 1741 during the Battle of Cartagena de Indias during the [War of Jenkins' Ear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_Jenkins'_Ear "War of Jenkins' Ear").
According to Augustine Sr's will, if his son Lawrence died without children, the Little Hunting Creek property would go to Augustine Jr., and Augustine Jr, in turn, would have to give up the Popes Creek property to his brother George. If Augustine Jr. did not want the Little Hunting Creek property, George would then inherit it. Upon Lawrence's death, Augustine Jr. chose Popes Creek and its slaves over the former Little Hunting Creek property. Lawrence's only surviving child, Sarah, lived until 1754; therefore, George Washington ultimately inherited the Little Hunting Creek property, which was known as Mount Vernon by that time. At his death, Augustine Washington Sr. enslaved a total of 64 people who were assigned among the various plantations.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustine_Washington#cite_note-Slavery_at_Popes_Creek_Plantation-12)

## Early and family life
Lawrence Washington's widow, Ann, had a life interest in the Little Hunting Creek plantation. Because she remarried and was not living at Mount Vernon, she leased the property to George in 1754. Upon her death in 1761, George Washington inherited the plantation outright.

**Augustine Washington, Sr.** (12 November 1694–12 April 1743), was an British colonial American planter and iron ore miner. He was the father of George Washington, the first president of the United States. He belonged to the Colony of Virginia's landed gentry. Like his father and his sons, Washington had owned plantations which he operated by the use of enslaved labor. He also speculated in less developed land and had even operated in an iron mine. Unlike his father and his son George, Washington was never a legislator. He held various offices in the counties where he had land.
Washington's first wife was Jane Butler, who died in November of 1729. His second wife was Mary Ball Washington, the mother of George Washington. He was the son of Lawrence Washington and his wife, Mildred Gale.

[An elaborate gravestone. A tribute from a grieving husband. But no name! For 210 years, Alexandria’s mysterious “Female Stranger” has inspired a question: Who was she? Her gravestone records that she died on October 14, 1816, aged 23 years and eight months. It describes a “disconsolate husband” in whose arms she “sighed out her latest breath.” Then comes the legend: a mysterious couple at Alexandria’s City Hotel, a young woman dying in Room 8, and a husband who is said to have sworn those caring for her never to reveal her name. How much of that story is true? We don’t know. Gadsby’s Tavern Museum’s research traces a newspaper account to 1866, fifty years after her death. No surviving hotel records confirm her stay. Some have suggested she was Aaron Burr’s daughter, Theodosia Burr Alston. But Theodosia disappeared at sea in 1813, nearly four years before the death recorded here. She also would have been 33, not 23. It’s a great story but highly improbable. But the legend has grown. The gravestone remains. And the woman it commemorates has never been conclusively identified. You can find her grave in St. Paul’s Episcopal Cemetery in Alexandria, Virginia. [What changes can a homeowner make to a historic home in the historic district of Old Town Alexandria? The answer is surprisingly simple and also less restrictive than people might think. If you own a historic home in Old Town Alexandria, there are not many interior restrictions without a specific architectural easement. Bob Weinhagen, President of Historic Alexandria Foundation (HAF) takes a moment to explain this. Home exteriors have more protection through Alexandria’s Board of Architectural Review (BAR). But Bob calls the interior “the wild west”! Bob is also the author of a new book called Old Town Style: Inside Alexandria’s Most Beautiful Historic Homes. Alexandria History Tours is proud to partner and support HAF and its mission to raise awareness and promote the preservation of historic properties in Old Town Alexandria. HAF is 501(c)(3) tax exempt membership organization. The mission is as follows: “The primary activities of the Foundation are education, advocacy, technical and easement advice, preservation grants, recognition awards and the historic plaque program. Since its founding, HAF has helped protect and preserve hundreds of irreplaceable buildings and artifacts associated with the city of Alexandria.” Considering the lack of restrictions on the interior of homes, the HAF mission is vital to preserving the historic character of beautiful Old Town Alexandria. Old Town Alexandria’s historic district is the third oldest historic district in the United States and it was established in 1946. We will continue a collaboration with Historic Alexandria Foundation to raise awareness and educate the public on Alexandria’s history, preservation, and the ongoing work to preserve Alexandria’s incredible history which is evident by the many historic and beautiful homes throughout Old Town Alexandria.

**Augustine Washington, Sr.** (12 November 1694–12 April 1743), was an British colonial American planter and iron ore miner. He was the father of George Washington, the first president of the United States. He belonged to the Colony of Virginia's landed gentry. Like his father and his sons, Washington had owned plantations which he operated by the use of enslaved labor. He also speculated in less developed land and had even operated in an iron mine. Unlike his father and his son George, Washington was never a legislator. He held various offices in the counties where he had land.
Washington's first wife was Jane Butler, who died in November of 1729. His second wife was Mary Ball Washington, the mother of George Washington. He was the son of Lawrence Washington and his wife, Mildred Gale.
